summary: Language models can turn radiology, pathology and discharge texts, including German ones, into tables at about the accuracy of a single human reader when the fact is stated plainly and the question is narrow (often 90 to 98%). Large open models that run inside the hospital match GPT-class models in several studies, while small or strongly compressed models are clearly worse. Accuracy drops for interpretation, rare diseases, free coding to terminologies, missing information, real scans, and probably at a new hospital. The best documented use is a person checking pre-filled answers, which was faster and more accurate than manual chart review in small studies. Systematic reviews agree that external validation is rare, and no pooled accuracy estimate for clinical text extraction was found.

findings.claim: A Münster team pulled 14 heart-function values out of 497 German cardiac MRI reports with off-the-shelf open models, with no fine-tuning.
findings.detail: Llama 3, Gemma, Mistral and Mixtral were tested on differently worded reports (for example LV-EF, RV-EF). Best values were 95.4% right annotation and 99.8% entity recognition accuracy. Numeric, explicitly stated values are the easy end of the task. The Münster link comes from an affiliation search match (authors Plagwitz, Neuhaus, Varghese and others).
findings.number: 95.4% right annotation, 99.8% NER accuracy (best); n=497 reports
findings.quote: The results strongly recommend using open-source LLMs for extracting medical parameters from clinical texts, including those in German
findings.source: Plagwitz et al., Zero-Shot LLMs for Named Entity Recognition: Targeting Cardiac Function Indicators in German Clinical Texts, Stud Health Technol Inform
findings.talk_use: Local opener: this already worked in Münster on German reports in 2024.

findings.claim: On German oncology imaging reports, local models matched humans on 'is there a metastasis?' but not on 'did the tumour respond?'.
findings.detail: 400 reports from 317 patients (Swiss tertiary hospital), 300 in the test set, five local models, duplicate human extraction with adjudication. Metastasis: humans 98.4%, gpt-oss:120b 97.6%. Response: humans 86.0%, best model 78.3%. Humans themselves agreed on only 76.2% for response versus 96.6% for metastasis. The models saw each report without earlier imaging.
findings.quote: LLMs were noninferior to human accuracy for classification of metastasis status but were inferior for response to treatment assessment
findings.source: Passweg et al., Data Extraction From Oncology Imaging Reports by Large Language Models: A Comparative Accuracy Study, JCO Clin Cancer Inform
findings.talk_use: Best single slide for research use: explicit facts are nearly solved, interpretation is not, for models and for people.

findings.claim: When experts re-checked cases in which the best local model disagreed with the human gold standard, the gold standard was judged wrong in about 20% of them.
findings.detail: Blinded oncologists reviewed discrepancies with gpt-oss:120b in the same study. Against the corrected reference the model became noninferior for treatment response. Only model-human disagreements were re-checked, so the correction can only favour the model.
findings.source: Passweg et al., JCO Clin Cancer Inform
findings.talk_use: Supports the chain of proof: both sides err, so every value needs a link back to its sentence.

findings.claim: Human coders needed about 2 minutes per German imaging report; local models needed 11 to 63 seconds.
findings.detail: Human time was estimated from REDCap audit logs (range 60 to 240 s). Model time depends on hardware and excludes building and checking the pipeline.
findings.number: about 120 s vs 11-63 s per report
findings.source: Passweg et al., JCO Clin Cancer Inform
findings.talk_use: Q&A number for effort on German data; small per report, large across thousands of reports.

findings.claim: On German chest X-ray reports, an open model without training clearly beat the rule-based system, and a modest number of labelled reports improved results further.
findings.detail: Retrospective study, University Hospital Bonn, 18,500 German and 3,927 English reports, 17 open models. German zero-shot macro F1: Mistral-Large 91.6% vs rules 74.8%. With 1,000 training reports: 94.3% vs BERT 86.7%; from 2,000 reports the gap to BERT was no longer relevant. The abstract reports the GPT-4o comparison on the public English set only (92.4% vs Mistral-Large 92.6%).
findings.quote: privacy-ensuring open-weights LLMs being competitive with closed-weights GPT-4o
findings.source: Nowak et al., Privacy-ensuring Open-weights LLMs Are Competitive with Closed-weights GPT-4o, Radiology
findings.talk_use: Answer to 'must we send data to OpenAI?': in this task local models were on par. Parity was tested on English reports.

findings.claim: A local 2023 model structured chest X-ray reports about as well as individual human readers, in both English and German.
findings.detail: Llama-2-70B, 202 English and 197 German reports, 48-item template, output restricted to allowed options. MCC English 0.75 vs readers 0.74/0.74; German 0.66 vs readers 0.67/0.66. German was harder for the humans too. The model sometimes invented pleural drains. Single prompt, small sample.
findings.quote: Locally hosted, open-source LLMs can automatically structure free-text radiology reports with approximately human accuracy
findings.source: Woźnicki et al., Automatic structuring of radiology reports with on-premise open-source LLMs, Eur Radiol
findings.talk_use: Human readers also disagree with a reference standard; the honest benchmark is the human.

findings.claim: A fine-tuned model in Essen looked near perfect on synthetic discharge letters but clearly weaker when physicians checked real ones.
findings.detail: MedGemma 27B was trained on 75,000 synthetic German cancer letters generated from FHIR data of 41,175 patients, with FHIR-compatible output. Synthetic test F1: 0.99 medication, 0.99 tumour, 0.84 ICD, 0.63 OPS codes. Physicians and a medical student on 30 real letters: 93.0% medication, 86.1% tumour, 78.9% ICD diagnoses, 61.3% procedures. Metrics differ (F1 vs correctness), so the drop is indicative. Single site.
findings.quote: procedure-related output should be treated as a structured draft that supports rather than replaces expert coding
findings.source: Eryılmaz et al. (University Hospital Essen), J Med Internet Res 2026, e92413
findings.talk_use: Best example from a German university hospital with FHIR output, and a warning against demo numbers.

findings.claim: On 21,364 real German pathology reports, five local models were not good enough for unsupervised tumour coding.
findings.detail: 10,823 patients, 2013 to 2025, self-hosted models. Exact ICD-O topography F1 71.6% (Qwen3-235B); exact morphology F1 only 34.7% (77.8% for the first three characters). Large gap between micro and macro averages: rare tumours were handled poorly.
findings.quote: performance is not yet sufficient for fully automated, unsupervised use in routine clinical workflows
findings.source: Arzideh et al., Automated Tumor ICD Coding of Real-World Pathology Reports, JCO Clin Cancer Inform 10:e2500254
findings.talk_use: Counterexample slide: large, real, German, and disappointing. Rare diseases are the weak spot.

findings.claim: A preprint with Dresden authors reports near-perfect extraction of 15 items from German liver cancer pathology reports with a local 31B model.
findings.detail: Two stages: a small gatekeeper model found the HCC cases among 2,864 reports with no errors and corrected wrong administrative metadata; Gemma 4 (31B) then extracted 15 variables, macro F1 above 0.99. One tumour type, not peer reviewed; the Dresden attribution is inferred from author names. Contrast with 34.7% for open-ended morphology coding in Essen: narrow schema versus a very large code list.
findings.quote: virtually eliminated objective factual errors
findings.source: Koch et al., LLMs for Structured Information Extraction from German Histopathology Reports: Hepatocellular Carcinoma, medRxiv
findings.talk_use: Newest German result; a narrow, well-defined question makes the difference.

findings.claim: For German prostate cancer pathology reports, a large local model equalled GPT-4; smaller or compressed models fell far behind.
findings.detail: 579 reports from 340 patients, 11 items, German and English versions. German zero-shot accuracy: GPT-4 97%, Llama 3 70B 97%, Llama 3 8B 83% (59% when compressed to 4 bit), Llama 2 13B 31%. Invented answers on 10 benign reports: GPT-4 none, Llama 3 70B about 2%, Llama 3 8B about 6%. No separate human comparator. One language version was produced by machine translation (search summary).
findings.quote: the performance of quantized model versions is not yet satisfactory
findings.source: Grothey et al., Comprehensive testing of LLMs for extraction of structured data in pathology, Commun Med 5:96
findings.talk_use: Same letter, very different results by model: model choice and size belong in the methods section.

findings.claim: Models confused 'pN1' (cancer in lymph nodes) with 'Pn1' (cancer along nerves), a difference only in capital letters.
findings.detail: Error analysis in the Cologne prostate pathology study: pN1 was reported when only perineural invasion Pn1 was in the text and pN was missing. A reader with the source line next to the value can spot this at once.
findings.quote: the models often confused lymph node status (pN) with perineural invasion (Pn) status
findings.source: Grothey et al., Commun Med 5:96
findings.talk_use: Most intuitive failure example for bio-scientists, and a direct argument for showing the source line next to each value.

findings.claim: The Dresden group made the model write down the supporting sentence before its yes/no answer, so every value carries its evidence.
findings.detail: Llama 2, 500 MIMIC-IV histories, five signs of decompensated cirrhosis, three blinded experts as reference. Example: the quoted sentence becomes abdominal pain, present = true. 70B sensitivity/specificity: cirrhosis 100/96, ascites 95/95, confusion 76/94. Output format was enforced by a grammar. English data only. The quoted sentence is a format example from the paper.
findings.quote: Patient reported mild right upper quadrant pain.
findings.source: Wiest et al., Privacy-preserving LLMs for structured medical information retrieval, npj Digit Med 7
findings.talk_use: Worked example text to data: sentence, field, value, evidence. Chain of proof in one line.

findings.claim: A small model stated that a patient was confused at admission although the report said nothing about it.
findings.detail: Same study, 7B model. Features that are described indirectly (confusion, breathlessness) were worst. Chain-of-thought prompting lowered ascites accuracy by about 25 points in the 7B model.
findings.quote: She had confusion present at admission
findings.source: Wiest et al., npj Digit Med
findings.talk_use: Concrete hallucination for a lay audience; a required quote that must exist in the text exposes it.

findings.claim: In a scan-to-data pipeline some wrong values came from the scan reading step and the language model repeated them.
findings.detail: LLM-AIx (open source, local): 100 TCGA colorectal pathology reports, Llama 3.1 70B, overall accuracy 87%, 88% after correcting errors in the human reference, 89% with another OCR engine. OCR also turned I/IV into 1/9.
findings.quote: “N1” was recognized as “N:”, “MA” was recognized as “M1”
findings.source: Wiest et al., A software pipeline for medical information extraction with LLMs, npj Precis Oncol 9:313
findings.talk_use: Explains why old scanned letters are a separate problem: errors enter before the language model reads.

findings.claim: A German form reader trained on synthetic care-transfer sheets lost 12 points when it met real scans.
findings.detail: University of Applied Sciences and University Hospital Augsburg; LayoutParser plus Tesseract, output to FHIR PIO-ULB, trained on 10,000 synthetic forms. Accuracy 97% synthetic, 85% real. First page of one form layout only.
findings.quote: Lower performance on real-world data was attributed to layout variability and scanning artifacts
findings.source: Werlitz et al., GMDS 2025, Stud Health Technol Inform, doi 10.3233/SHTI251392
findings.talk_use: German example for paper forms to FHIR; the route exists, real layouts are the obstacle.

findings.claim: Small image-reading language models transcribed photographed clinical reports with far fewer errors than classic OCR.
findings.detail: 340 photographed obstetric ultrasound reports from India, 60 hand-transcribed for testing. Character error rate: Tesseract 18.9%, Qwen-2.5 VL 3.1%. Numeric accuracy over 92%, so a relevant share of numbers may still be wrong. Preprint, English, not hospital letters.
findings.quote: MLLMs achieve over 92% numeric accuracy
findings.source: Neveditsin et al., Compact Multimodal Language Models as Robust OCR Alternatives, arXiv 2511.13523
findings.talk_use: Old scans are becoming readable on local hardware; numbers still need checks.

findings.claim: Much of the disagreement between differently worded prompts comes from one distinction: 'the note says no' versus 'the note says nothing'.
findings.detail: MIMIC-IV discharge summaries, 17 fields with yes/no/not documented, three prompt wordings, two model sizes; median kappa 0.69 and 0.68 across prompts. Merging no and not documented removed most disagreement. Changing the model altered the main admission category on close to half of notes, rewording the prompt on about one in eight. Single author, no human reference.
findings.number: model change: close to half; prompt change: about 1 in 8
findings.quote: changing the model reassigns the dominant tag on close to half of all notes
findings.source: Murin, Measuring the sensitivity of LLM-based structured extraction, arXiv 2606.05970
findings.talk_use: Key concept for doctoral candidates: define 'not documented' in the codebook, and fix model and prompt version.

findings.claim: Filling case report forms from notes remains hard: the winning system in a 2026 shared task reached macro F1 0.68, and a local Munich system 0.55.
findings.detail: CL4Health 2026 CRF filling, English emergency notes. 96.3% of training labels were 'unknown', so systems must mostly keep silent. TUM system (MedGemma 27B): a first step that asks 'is it mentioned?' raised development F1 from 0.33 to 0.42. Negated mentions were still misread as positive.
findings.quote: Reliably distinguishing between a ruled-out label and missing information remains a known difficulty in clinical NLP
findings.source: Sommer et al. (TUM), sebis at CRF Filling 2026, arXiv 2606.13082
findings.talk_use: Reality check for anyone hoping to auto-fill a CRF with 100 fields.

findings.claim: Frontier models asked to write SNOMED CT codes from memory produced non-existent codes in 11% to 19% of cases; a lookup step removed almost all of these, but the choice of code stayed poor.
findings.detail: SNOMED CT Entity Linking Challenge, GPT-5.2, Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.5. Micro hallucination rate 10.89% to 19.34% without retrieval (body text), close to zero with retrieval; F1 with retrieval 19% to 23%, versus 78% for the specialised KIRI system. Authors work for a vendor (Emtelligent) whose own system scores best in the paper.
findings.number: 10.9-19.3% invented codes; close to 0% with lookup
findings.quote: LLMs hallucinate medical codes at a rate that currently renders them unsuitable for autonomous clinical coding applications
findings.source: Born et al., Profiling Hallucinations in Frontier LLMs for Entity Linking to Medical Ontologies, ClinicalNLP @ LREC 2026
findings.talk_use: Let the model find the phrase and a terminology service find the code.

findings.claim: Clinicians who reviewed charts with a local model's pre-filled answers were both faster and more accurate than without it.
findings.detail: Mount Sinai, four clinicians, 38 patients, MedGemma 27B. Manual 68% (142/207) correct vs assisted 89% (185/207); median 9.4 vs 3.6 minutes per patient. In a separate benchmark the model alone averaged 69.3%. Invented values 1.2% (13/1063). Reference by one clinician. Values the model missed stay invisible to the reviewer.
findings.quote: human verification remains essential to ensure correctness
findings.source: Neuse et al., Cutting chart-review time and improving database accuracy in IBD with human-in-the-loop LLMs, BMC Med Inform Decis Mak
findings.talk_use: Headline for research use: human plus AI beat human alone. Do not plot 69% next to 68/89 without saying it is a separate benchmark.

findings.claim: An LLM chart-review tool was more accurate than one manual reviewer, and the reviewer with AI help was best.
findings.detail: Columbia University, 91 patients, about 5,834 documents. Accuracy: manual 82.3%, tool 94.3%, AI-assisted 97.1%. Time per chart: 25.2 min, 80 s, 8.8 min. Cost about $0.20 per 2,000-word chunk. Reference: consensus of three reviewers; the manual comparator was a single clinician; abstract and text give inconsistent details (83% vs 82.28%; 16, 20 or 21 variables).
findings.quote: OphthoACR achieved 94% accuracy in extracting variables of interest, significantly outperforming manual review (83%).
findings.source: Chen et al., OphthoACR, Transl Vis Sci Technol 14(10):8
findings.talk_use: Second, independent human-plus-AI example, for Q&A on cost and time.

findings.claim: A general enterprise assistant with one fixed prompt reached 92% to 94% exact agreement with human abstractors and had to show the text snippet for each value.
findings.detail: 26 patients, 130 data points, one centre, Microsoft Copilot. Manual about 30 min per patient, AI 2 to 3 min plus verification. The prompt required 'Not documented' when a value was missing and a supporting snippet for each value. No invented values. Very small.
findings.quote: these findings should be interpreted as a feasibility assessment rather than evidence of generalizable performance
findings.source: Schwartz et al., JMIR Form Res 2026, e96755
findings.talk_use: Two prompt rules anyone can copy: allow 'not documented', demand the snippet.

findings.claim: A 2026 systematic review found best-model accuracies of 88% to 97% for breast pathology reports, with almost no testing at other hospitals.
findings.detail: Nine studies, seven databases up to December 2025, PRISMA and PROBAST+AI. Only one study had external validation. One included study lost 11 to 32 percentage points from curated test cases to real documents. Tumour location reached only 63.8% in one study. No pooling because tasks and metrics differ.
findings.number: 87.7-97.4%; drop of 11-32 points curated to real
findings.quote: published performance metrics should be interpreted cautiously when planning clinical deployment
findings.source: Shankar et al., Performance of LLMs for extracting clinical data from breast cancer pathology reports: a systematic review, npj Digit Med
findings.talk_use: The summary number to quote, together with its warning.

findings.claim: For breast cancer histology reports, two large models scored the same as a trained human annotator; smaller ones did not.
findings.detail: English reports, agreement with a gold standard: human annotator 95.4%, GPT-4o 96.1%, Llama 3.1 405B 94.7% (differences not significant), Llama 3.1 70B 91.6%, GPT-4o mini 87.9%. The large models also cost more per report.
findings.source: Balasubramanian et al., Leveraging LLMs for structured information extraction from pathology reports, arXiv 2502.12183 (J Pathol Inform 2025)
findings.talk_use: Clean comparison against a human who is also imperfect (95.4%).

findings.claim: A JAMIA review of text mining for clinical registries found 15 studies, only one of which used generative LLMs, and most had a high risk of bias.
findings.detail: 2010 to 2025. Median micro F1 81.2% (45.5 to 94.9). 11 of 15 without external validation, 9 of 15 high risk of bias, 5 report real-world use. The single generative LLM study is German (50 pathology documents).
findings.number: median F1 81.2%; 9/15 high risk of bias
findings.quote: most systems remain experimental rather than ready for routine use in clinical registry settings
findings.source: Liu et al., Using NLP to extract information from clinical text for populating clinical registries: a systematic review, JAMIA, doi 10.1093/jamia/ocaf176
findings.talk_use: Honest state of evidence for registries such as tumour documentation.

findings.claim: Giving the model the same written annotation rules that human coders use raised its precision strongly on stroke CT reports.
findings.detail: Preprint from a single academic stroke centre (Munich), ten findings, datasets of 200 and 100 reports. Dataset B precision GPT-4o 0.83 to 0.95, Llama-3.3-70B 0.87 to 0.94; infarct demarcation 0.59 to 1.00 as the largest gain. Recall hardly changed.
findings.quote: well-defined annotation guidelines can enhance LLM data extraction accuracy
findings.source: Wihl et al., Data Extraction from Free-Text Stroke CT Reports Using GPT-4o and Llama-3.3-70B, medRxiv
findings.talk_use: A good codebook improves the result, and researchers already know how to write one.

findings.claim: Classic trained text models can still beat large language models when enough labelled data exist, and translating clinical text to English first makes results worse.
findings.detail: DRAGON benchmark (28 Dutch clinical tasks): trained RoBERTa 0.819 vs best zero-shot LLM (Llama 3.3 70B) 0.760, although the LLM won 14 tasks and RoBERTa 11. In German, 7B models (Hamburg, KONVENS 2025, https://aclanthology.org/2025.konvens-1.4.pdf) lost to baselines on the baselines' own dataset but won on unfamiliar data; drug F1 0.71 to 0.87, diagnoses and treatments 0.44 to 0.71.
findings.quote: Translation to English prior to inference consistently degraded performance
findings.source: Builtjes et al., Leveraging Open-Source LLMs for Clinical Information Extraction, arXiv 2507.20859; Spiegel et al., KONVENS 2025
findings.talk_use: Q&A: do we always need an LLM? No. And do not translate German letters first.

findings.claim: When local models got a first-diagnosis date wrong in German urology notes, they were off by a median of more than four years.
findings.detail: 149 snippets, 11 open models. Best model 92% correct dates (Mistral NeMo 12B), ICD-10 above 85%. 37 snippets contained no tumour; some models still named one. Authors judge about 90% not yet suitable for real use.
findings.number: 92% correct; median error 1,520 days among wrong answers
findings.quote: the median error across all wrong LLM responses was 1,520 days
findings.source: Can open source LLMs be used for tumor documentation in Germany?, BioData Mining 18:48
findings.talk_use: Errors are rare but not small; an average accuracy hides this.

findings.claim: Doctors who used an AI chart summary in the record complained about missing facts far more often than about invented ones.
findings.detail: US evaluation, 10 physicians, 147 summaries with free-text feedback: 46 omissions, 5 hallucinations or errors, 27 token-limit comments. One summary turned severe aortic stenosis into moderate. This is summarisation, so adjacent to extraction.
findings.quote: Cards visit assessment noted "Severe" AS - summary said moderate AS.
findings.source: Kahl et al., Evaluation of electronic health record-integrated AI chart review, npj Health Systems
findings.talk_use: Chain of proof catches invented facts; it does not catch missing ones. Coverage needs its own check.

caveats: Accuracy numbers from different studies cannot be compared: tasks, fields, metrics and reference standards differ.
Human gold standards contain errors (about 20% of re-checked disagreements in Passweg 2026), so measured accuracy can be too low; where the reference was built with model help it can be too high.
Evidence for time saved is mostly small, single-centre and not randomised; time to build, validate and monitor the pipeline is usually not counted.
A quoted source sentence exposes invented values but not omissions.
Many results come from outdated models (Llama 2/3); results of small models do not carry over to large ones.

Nowak, Arzideh, Plagwitz, Koch, Wihl, Werlitz and Murin were read as abstracts (Werlitz and Murin plus opening pages). Full texts of PMC articles were read through a summarising fetch tool; check quotes against the original before putting them on a slide.
Born et al. have a vendor interest.
gaps: No pooled meta-analysis of LLM extraction accuracy from clinical text found.
No published evaluation of vision-language models on scanned German Arztbriefe or ePA PDFs found, and none on documents from ORBIS.
Table extraction from clinical PDFs: no suitable clinical evaluation found.
Only one Münster study found (cardiac MRI, 2024); RACOON text extraction was not searched.
No longitudinal study of model drift or version change in hospital extraction found; only a model-swap comparison (Murin 2026).
No cost comparison including validation work and no randomised trial of assisted chart review found.
Bias by sex or ethnicity in extraction is named as a risk but not quantified in the sources read.
OMOP mapping and long-document effects: no strong extraction study read.

Aachen, Freiburg and Charité: Europe PMC searches gave no further German extraction study beyond shared authorship and a Freiburg GPT-4o neurosurgery feasibility study (not read). LMU (Wang 2024: up to 90%, 800 reports) and Essen/Aachen GPT-4 letters (Siepmann 2025: 20 patients) were seen as abstract or search summary only.
